- **Archive parent:** Fuzz
- **Builder:** Aul Instruments
- **Catalog type:** Fuzz
- **Identity:** Very early fuzz boxes made by Aul Instruments for Mike Matthews in 1967, before Electro-Harmonix, closely derived from the Mosrite Fuzzrite family and associated historically with the Guild Foxey Lady replacement program. [1][2]

Effects Database places the Aul fuzzes in the early history of Mike Matthews' pre-Electro-Harmonix work. Fuzzboxes documents the surviving Aul examples as close to the early Fuzzrite design, including the characteristic compact folded-metal construction. [1][2]

- Produced around **1967**.
- Built for Mike Matthews before the Electro-Harmonix brand launched.
- Connected to Guild's replacement for the Foxey Lady after Mosrite's bankruptcy.
- Related Aul-built examples later appeared under the **Guild Foxey Lady** name. [1][3]

- Surviving Aul/Guild-family documentation supports a simple vintage fuzz control arrangement.
- The Guild Foxey Lady AUL version is documented with **Volume** and **Tone**, with the Volume control also acting as the switching control. [3]
- Exact control layouts are not fully preserved for every unbranded Aul example.

- **Primary lineage:** Mosrite Fuzzrite.
- The surviving evidence supports a close Fuzzrite-derived design rather than an unrelated original topology. [2]

- **Technology:** Silicon.
- Surviving Aul examples are documented with unmarked metal-can silicon transistors.
- Exact transistor part numbers are not established.

- Exact clipping diode/device is not publicly documented.

- **Greenish-grey wrinkle finish** is documented on surviving Aul examples.
- Folded metal enclosure.
- Some units have Manny's stickers reflecting period distribution. [2]

- The important historical distinction is the transition from Aul Instruments production to the later Guild/Electro-Harmonix Foxey Lady lineage.
- No numbered Aul hardware revision sequence is established.

- The reviewed historical sources point to vintage **battery-powered** operation, but do not preserve a complete standardized electrical specification for every surviving example.

The Aul design belongs to the early Fuzzrite sound family, with a direct two-transistor silicon fuzz character. Exact response can vary between surviving examples because individual component identities and bias conditions are not fully documented. [1][2]

- **Identity / 1967 context:** High
- **Fuzzrite lineage:** High
- **Silicon transistor technology:** High
- **Greenish-grey wrinkle finish:** High for surviving examples
- **Guild Foxey Lady relationship:** High
- **Exact transistor:** Unknown
- **Exact diode:** Unknown
- **Universal power specification:** Not established

Effects Database, Fuzzboxes and the historical Guild Foxey Lady record were cross-checked. The evidence supports Aul Instruments as an early Mike Matthews production source, establishes the close Fuzzrite lineage and preserves the greenish-grey wrinkle-finish/silicon-transistor context. The archive avoids assigning exact transistor part numbers where the surviving evidence does not identify them. [1][2][3]

1. Effects Database — Aul Instruments Fuzz: https://www.effectsdatabase.com/model/aul/fuzz
2. Fuzzboxes — Mosrite Fuzzrite history / Aul Instruments: https://fuzzboxes.org/features/fuzzrite
3. Effects Database — Guild Foxey Lady: https://www.effectsdatabase.com/model/guild/foxeylady

Mosrite Fuzzrite: A detailed history Background Myth-busting Analysis of the Fuzzrite’s graphics Tech specs Perf board Fuzzrite ‘Reversed’ Fuzzrite Conventional germanium Fuzzrite Eyelet board Fuzzrite Silicon transistor Fuzzrite Guild Foxey Lady (Mosrite version) Production numbers Future of the Fuzzrite Sierra & Rosac Electronics Moseley pedals Aul Instruments fuzz Electro-Harmonix pedals Obscure east coast fuzz (Manny’s, Orpheum etc.) Background The Mosrite guitar company was founded in Bakersfield, CA, in 1956, by brothers Semie & Andy Moseley, thanks to an investment from Ray Boatright. The name, ‘Mosrite’, was a portmanteau of these two entities. It wasn’t until Mosrite assembly-line inspector, Eugene Moles, met Nokie Edwards in the early 1960s, that the company became involved with the Ventures, and ultimately started offering the various signature models. 1 Ed Sanner was reputedly involved with Mosrite by 1965, developing circuits for a range of amplifiers that they planned on offering, in addition to the guitars. 2 Sanner recalls supplying steel guitar player, Leo LeBlanc, with a custom-made fuzzbox, and subsequently Semie became interested in manufacturing this as what would eventually become the Mosrite Fuzzrite. 3 It is unknown exactly when the Fuzzrite came on the market. Over the course of several years, the Fuzzrite underwent numerous cosmetic changes, as well as technical changes to the circuit. Analysis of surviving Fuzzrite pedals suggests that production of Mosrite’s fuzz box began at some point in mid-to-late 1966, and continued through 1968, presumably until the time when the company infamously went bankrupt. Despite a relatively short-lived original production run, the Fuzzrite proved to be an influential fuzz box design, and it spawned numerous imitations, as well as official reissues, over the years and decades to come. Myth-busting There are two distinctly different versions of the Mosrite Fuzzrite that were being built during the period of 1966-1968. Earlier Fuzzrites were built with a set of 2N2613 & 2N408 germanium transistors, while later versions used silicon transistors, across a variety of different construction methods. For a long time, there was a common belief circulating the various Internet forums that the earlier, germanium-transistor Fuzzrites were built in considerably smaller numbers than the silicon versions. Ed Sanner recalled Mosrite having shipped “around 200 [Fuzzrites]” before they realised that the innate temperature-sensitivity of germanium transistors was leading to problems with the fuzz sound. 4 In another interview, at some point in the early 2000s, Sanner also gave the number of germanium-transistor Fuzzrites produced, as ‘250’, and cited the same problem of temperature-sensitivity being the catalyst for the move to the silicon-transistor design. 5 Extensive study of the technical details of the germanium version of the Fuzzrite casts some doubt over this narrative. The following sections explore the development of the germanium-transistor Fuzzrite in greater detail, and furthers the possibility that this ‘temperature-sensitive’ model is not quite as rare as some dealers and collectors like to think. Analysis of the Fuzzrite’s graphics Before diving into the technical specifications of the various different versions of the Mosrite Fuzzrite, it’s useful to examine the way that screen-printed graphics on the Fuzzrite casings changed over the years. This is because the changes Mosrite made to the graphics on the enclosures generally correlate with the changes that Mosrite made to the circuitry inside, and with the date codes stamped on components.
